Vignette:
A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 11.2%) presents with rapidly worsening pain, swelling, and redness of his right lower leg that began 2 days ago after a minor abrasion he sustained while gardening. Despite oral cephalexin started by his PCP yesterday, the erythema has expanded dramatically. On examination, he appears toxic and diaphoretic. Vital signs: T 39.8C, HR 128, RR 24, BP 92/56, SpO2 95%. The right leg demonstrates tense, dusky erythema extending from the ankle to the knee with areas of purplish discoloration and hemorrhagic bullae. Crepitus is palpable along the anterior shin. Pain is severe and extends beyond the visible margins of erythema. Labs: WBC 28,200/mcL, glucose 428 mg/dL, sodium 131 mEq/L, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, CRP 32 mg/dL, lactate 4.6 mmol/L. LRINEC score is 10. CT of the leg shows extensive gas tracking along the fascial planes.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 55-year-old
Sex: Male
Complaint: Rapidly worsening pain, swelling, and redness of the right lower leg with fever, hypotension, and confusion/toxic appearance.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for necrotizing fasciitis of the right lower extremity complicated by septic shock. The strongest supporting facts are: rapidly progressive soft tissue infection despite oral cephalexin; severe pain extending beyond the visible margins of erythema; hemorrhagic bullae and dusky/purplish discoloration; palpable crepitus; CT demonstrating extensive gas tracking along fascial planes; LRINEC score of 10 indicating high risk; and systemic sepsis with fever (39.8°C), tachycardia (128 bpm), tachypnea (24/min), hypotension (92/56 mmHg), and hyperlactatemia (4.6 mmol/L). Laboratory data also reveal leukocytosis (WBC 28,200/mcL), acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.4 mg/dL), hyponatremia (131 mEq/L), and severe hyperglycemia (glucose 428 mg/dL). The main differential includes severe cellulitis or clostridial myonecrosis, but the combination of CT gas, crepitus, bullae, and pain out of proportion makes necrotizing fasciitis the unifying diagnosis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Blood cultures (obtained prior to antibiotics); emergent surgical exploration for definitive diagnosis and source control.
Conclusion: Necrotizing fasciitis of the right lower extremity with septic shock and acute kidney injury in a poorly controlled diabetic patient; this is a surgical emergency requiring immediate operative debridement, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and aggressive hemodynamic resuscitation.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery
Recommendations: Activate the surgical team immediately for emergent operative debridement without awaiting further imaging. Obtain blood cultures, then initiate broad-spectrum IV antibiotic coverage for polymicrobial infection including MRSA, streptococci, gram-negative organisms, and anaerobes. Begin aggressive isotonic fluid resuscitation for septic shock; if hypotension persists, initiate norepinephrine to maintain mean arterial pressure ≥65 mmHg. Admit to the intensive care unit for hemodynamic monitoring, serial lactate checks, and urine output monitoring. Initiate an insulin infusion to treat severe hyperglycemia and monitor/correct electrolytes, particularly in the setting of acute kidney injury. Ensure tetanus prophylaxis is addressed. Prepare for possible renal replacement therapy if indicated by progressive azotemia or electrolyte derangement.
Notes: Surgical exploration is the gold standard for diagnosis; operative intervention must not be delayed for additional laboratory or imaging studies.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 20-year-old male college athlete presents with itchy, peeling skin between his toes bilaterally for the past 2 weeks. He plays on the soccer team and uses communal showers at the athletic facility daily. He denies pain, swelling, or spreading beyond the interdigital spaces. He has no history of diabetes or immunosuppression. On examination, there is maceration and peeling of the skin in the third and fourth interdigital web spaces of both feet. Mild erythema is present. There are no vesicles, bullae, or fissures extending to the soles. Toenails appear normal.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 20-year-old
Sex: Male
Complaint: Itchy, peeling, macerated skin in the third and fourth interdigital web spaces of both feet for 2 weeks.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for interdigital tinea pedis (athlete’s foot). The strongest supporting facts are the patient’s status as a college soccer athlete, daily use of communal showers, bilateral involvement limited to the third and fourth toe webs, and physical findings of maceration with peeling and mild erythema confined to the interdigital spaces without extension to the soles. The absence of vesicles, bullae, fissures, nail changes, diabetes, or immunosuppression supports uncomplicated superficial fungal infection. The primary differential considerations include erythrasma (usually less pruritic and shows coral-red fluorescence on Wood’s lamp), gram-negative toe web infection (typically associated with marked malodor and often secondary changes), contact dermatitis (would be linked to new footwear or topical exposures and unlikely to localize so precisely to the web spaces), and juvenile plantar dermatosis (affects weight-bearing areas in younger children and is not applicable here). The site and character of maceration and peeling in the classic interdigital distribution favor tinea pedis.

A 14-year-old boy presents with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Eighteen hours earlier, he had been at a picnic where he ingested undercooked chicken along with a variety of other foods. He reports moderate-volume, nonbloody stools occurring 6 times a day. He has mild abdominal cramps and a low-grade fever. He is evaluated at an acute care clinic and found to be mildly tachycardic (heart rate 105 bpm) with a normal BP and a low-grade temperature of 100.1°F (37.8°C). His physical exam is unremarkable except for mild diffuse abdominal tenderness and mild increased bowel sounds. baseline_protocol:
Age: 14-year-old
Sex: Male
Complaint: Nausea, vomiting, nonbloody diarrhea (6 times daily), and mild abdominal cramps following ingestion of undercooked chicken 18 hours prior.
Analysis: The 18-hour incubation period and exposure to undercooked chicken are most consistent with invasive bacterial enteritis—such as nontyphoidal Salmonella or Campylobacter—rather than a preformed toxin-mediated illness, which typically presents within 1 to 6 hours. The presence of low-grade fever and abdominal cramps supports an infectious inflammatory process. The patient is hemodynamically stable with normal blood pressure, mild tachycardia, and intact oral tolerance, indicating mild dehydration without shock. The nonbloody, moderate-volume diarrhea and absence of severe or localized abdominal pain suggest uncomplicated disease. Differential considerations include Campylobacter jejuni, nontyphoidal Salmonella species, and less likely Clostridioides perfringens given the presence of fever. Viral etiologies and Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli are less consistent with the short incubation and specific food vehicle. No specified immunocompromising conditions or hemoglobinopathies place him at heightened risk for bacteremia or focal seeding.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Uncomplicated acute foodborne bacterial gastroenteritis, most likely due to nontyphoidal Salmonella or Campylobacter, in a stable adolescent following undercooked chicken exposure.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease
Recommendations: 1) Continue oral rehydration with an appropriate electrolyte solution to maintain hydration. 2) Withhold empiric antibiotics because uncomplicated nontyphoidal bacterial enteritis is self-limited, and antibiotics do not shorten illness while prolonging fecal carriage. 3) No immediate stool culture or molecular gastrointestinal panel is required, as results would not change management in this uncomplicated, clinically stable patient; reserve testing if symptoms persist beyond several days, worsen, bloody diarrhea develops, or public health investigation requires identification. 4) Report the suspected foodborne illness/outbreak to local public health authorities as mandated. 5) Monitor for red flags including bloody stools, high fever, severe or localized abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, worsening dehydration, or altered mental status, and return for care if these occur. 6) Maintain strict hand hygiene to prevent household transmission.
Notes: If fever increases or bloody diarrhea develops, avoid antimotility agents. The patient has no specified risk factors (e.g., immunocompromise, hemoglobinopathy, extreme age) that would increase concern for bacteremia or invasive complications.

Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman presents with a 9-month history of chronic watery diarrhea, abdominal bloating, and unintentional weight loss of 12 pounds. She reports 3 to 5 loose stools daily and intermittent crampy abdominal pain. She has also noticed increasing fatigue and occasional mouth sores. Her past medical history is unremarkable except for iron deficiency anemia diagnosed 6 months ago that has been poorly responsive to oral iron supplementation. On examination, she appears thin with a BMI of 18.5. She is pale. Abdominal examination reveals mild diffuse tenderness without organomegaly. There are no skin rashes. Laboratory results show hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL with a low MCV of 72, ferritin 8 ng/mL, and low serum vitamin D at 15 ng/mL. Tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody is elevated at 98 units (normal less than 20). Total IgA level is normal.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 28
Sex: Female
Complaint: Nine-month history of chronic watery diarrhea, abdominal bloating, unintentional weight loss of 12 pounds, intermittent crampy abdominal pain, increasing fatigue, and occasional mouth sores; complicated by iron deficiency anemia poorly responsive to oral iron supplementation.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for a malabsorptive small bowel process rather than a functional bowel disorder. Key supporting features include unintentional weight loss, iron deficiency anemia that has failed to respond to oral supplementation, and low vitamin D. The markedly elevated tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody (98 units, normal <20) in the presence of a normal total IgA level is highly specific for celiac disease. While inflammatory bowel disease, microscopic colitis, giardiasis, and thyroid disease can cause chronic diarrhea, they are unlikely given the refractory iron deficiency anemia, low vitamin D, and strongly positive celiac serology. Physical findings of pallor, low BMI, and mild diffuse tenderness are consistent with chronic malabsorption.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Upper endoscopy (esophagogastroduodenoscopy) with multiple duodenal biopsies for histopathologic confirmation.
Conclusion: Celiac disease is the unifying diagnosis based on chronic diarrhea, malabsorptive features, and elevated tTG IgA with normal total IgA; confirmation by endoscopic biopsy is required before initiating any dietary change.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology
Recommendations: 
1. Refer to Gastroenterology for upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsies to confirm celiac disease.
2. Instruct the patient to continue a regular gluten-containing diet until the procedure is completed to avoid false-negative histology.
3. Initiate vitamin D repletion for documented deficiency.
4. Continue current oral iron pending specialist evaluation; reassess iron stores after mucosal healing and implementation of a gluten-free diet.
5. Counsel that a gluten-free diet must not be started before confirmatory testing.
Notes: None

Age: 74
Sex: Female
Complaint: Acute confusion with retrograde amnesia following a nocturnal episode associated with oral bleeding from a tongue laceration, urinary incontinence, and bilateral upper extremity soreness.
Analysis: The presentation is most consistent with a first-time generalized tonic-clonic seizure with postictal confusion. The strongest supporting facts are the lateral tongue laceration (highly specific for seizure), urinary incontinence during sleep, witnessed nocturnal motor activity ("tossing around in bed"), bilateral arm pain consistent with postictal myalgias, and prolonged confusion/amnesia. The CT finding of an ill-defined rounded mass adjacent to the dura of the posterior falx indicates a structural intracranial lesion as the likely underlying cause. The normal awake EEG does not exclude epilepsy, as a single interictal recording can be normal. Metabolic or toxic etiologies are unlikely given a glucose of 70 mg/dL, near-normal sodium, normal calcium and magnesium, an alcohol level of 10 mg/dL, and a negative urine toxicology screen. Transient global amnesia is a less likely alternative because it is not associated with tongue biting, incontinence, or diffuse musculoskeletal soreness. Syncope would not explain the retrograde amnesia or lateral tongue bite.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: MRI of the brain with and without contrast to further characterize the posterior falx dural-based mass.
Conclusion: First-time unprovoked generalized tonic-clonic seizure in the setting of a posterior falx dural-based intracranial mass, presenting with postictal confusion, retrograde amnesia, and minor injuries.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Neurology
Recommendations: Admit for inpatient observation and urgent neurology consultation. Initiate seizure precautions and consider starting an anti-epileptic medication (e.g., levetiracetam) given the identified structural brain lesion. Obtain contrast-enhanced MRI to better define the nature and extent of the dural-based mass, with neurosurgical referral if significant mass effect or a resectable lesion is confirmed. Provide local wound care for the superficial tongue laceration and analgesia for bilateral arm soreness. Counsel the patient and family on seizure safety, strict avoidance of alcohol and sleep deprivation, and driving/height restrictions until cleared by neurology.
Notes: A normal interictal EEG does not rule out a seizure disorder, and a single normal awake EEG can be seen after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 38
Sex: Female
Complaint: Three-week history of persistent throat clearing and mild nocturnal cough with a sensation of mucus dripping in the back of the throat, following a resolved upper respiratory infection.
Analysis: The presentation is most consistent with upper airway cough syndrome (UACS) secondary to post-infectious/post-viral rhinitis. The strongest supporting finding is the cobblestone appearance of the posterior pharyngeal wall, a classic physical sign of chronic post-nasal drip. The clear, thin nasal secretions and mild mucosal erythema align with persistent post-viral rhinitis, and the temporal relationship to a recent cold supports this mechanism. The absence of fever, purulent nasal discharge, and sinus tenderness makes acute bacterial rhinosinusitis unlikely. The lack of wheezing and clear lungs on auscultation reduce the probability of cough-variant asthma, though it remains a relevant differential if the cough proves refractory to initial therapy. The denial of heartburn makes gastroesophageal reflux disease–related cough less likely, but silent reflux cannot be completely excluded. Nocturnal worsening is consistent with positional pooling of upper airway secretions.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Upper airway cough syndrome (UACS) due to post-infectious rhinitis, presenting as subacute cough and post-nasal drip.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology
Recommendations: Initiate empiric intranasal corticosteroid (e.g., fluticasone or mometasone) once daily and saline nasal irrigation twice daily. Elevate the head of the bed at night to reduce nocturnal pooling of secretions. Arrange follow-up in 2–4 weeks to confirm treatment response. If cough persists despite optimal nasal therapy, obtain spirometry before and after inhaled bronchodilator to exclude cough-variant asthma. If the cough remains refractory, reassess for gastroesophageal reflux disease. Because medication history was not provided, verify that the patient is not taking ACE inhibitors or other agents associated with drug-induced cough.
Notes: Medication history not specified.

First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. A 19-year-old tall, thin male (6'3", 145 lbs) presents with sudden onset of sharp right-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea that began 2 hours ago while playing basketball. He has no prior medical history, takes no medications, and does not smoke. On examination, he is mildly tachypneic but speaking in full sentences. Vital signs: T 36.8C, HR 104, RR 22, BP 128/76, SpO2 93% on room air. The right hemithorax is hyperresonant to percussion with decreased breath sounds on the right compared to the left. baseline_protocol:
Age: 19-year-old
Sex: Male
Complaint: Sudden onset sharp right-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea that began 2 hours ago while playing basketball.
Analysis: The patient is a tall, thin young male, the classic demographic for primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP). The presentation of acute pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea triggered by physical exertion, combined with ipsilateral hyperresonance and decreased breath sounds, strongly supports pneumothorax. Chest X-ray confirms a large right-sided pneumothorax with approximately 60% lung collapse and, importantly, no mediastinal shift, ruling out tension physiology. Vital signs show mild tachycardia, tachypnea, and mild hypoxemia (SpO2 93% on room air), indicating physiological compromise but hemodynamic stability. Relevant differential considerations include secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (unlikely given the absence of known lung disease), traumatic pneumothorax (no trauma reported), pulmonary embolism, and pleuritis, but the radiographic findings definitively establish PSP. The large size (>50% collapse) and ongoing symptoms mandate active intervention rather than observation alone.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Large right-sided primary spontaneous pneumothorax (~60% collapse) in a hemodynamically stable 19-year-old male without tension physiology.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology
Recommendations: Perform immediate small-bore chest tube thoracostomy (e.g., 14–20 Fr) to the right hemithorax to re-expand the lung given the large size and symptomatic presentation. Provide supplemental high-flow oxygen to accelerate pleural air reabsorption and administer adequate analgesia. Obtain a repeat chest X-ray after tube placement to confirm lung re-expansion and appropriate tube positioning. Admit for observation and monitoring for persistent air leak. Consult thoracic surgery if an air leak persists beyond 48 hours, if the lung fails to fully re-expand, or if recurrence is suspected. Instruct the patient to avoid strenuous exercise, air travel, and scuba diving until full resolution is confirmed at outpatient follow-up.
Notes: None

Vignette:
A 50-year-old woman presents with a 5-day history of persistent dizziness described as a sensation of spinning. She reports the dizziness is constant rather than positional and is accompanied by an unsteady gait and difficulty walking in a straight line. She has had two episodes of nausea and vomiting. She denies hearing loss or tinnitus. Past medical history is notable for migraine headaches and hypertension. On examination, vital signs are stable. Neurological exam reveals vertical nystagmus that does not suppress with fixation, mild dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing on the right, and gait ataxia with veering to the right. Hearing is intact bilaterally. Dix-Hallpike maneuver is negative.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 50-year-old
Sex: Woman
Complaint: Persistent spinning dizziness (vertigo) for 5 days with unsteady gait, difficulty walking straight, nausea and vomiting, and right-sided incoordination.
Analysis: This presentation is highly consistent with central vertigo due to a posterior fossa lesion. The strongest supporting facts are: (1) vertical nystagmus that does not suppress with fixation, which localizes to the brainstem or cerebellum and is not seen in peripheral vestibular disorders; (2) right-sided dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing, indicating right cerebellar hemisphere dysfunction; (3) gait ataxia with veering to the right, further supporting a right-sided cerebellar or brainstem process; (4) constant, non-positional vertigo with a negative Dix-Hallpike maneuver, effectively ruling out benign paroxysmal positional vertigo; and (5) intact bilateral hearing without tinnitus, making Ménière disease or labyrinthitis unlikely. In a 50-year-old with hypertension, the leading concern is a posterior circulation ischemic stroke (e.g., right cerebellar hemisphere or lateral medullary/brainstem infarction). Completed intracerebral hemorrhage, demyelinating disease, or neoplasm remain less likely but must be excluded with neuroimaging. Vestibular migraine is unlikely because of the objective cerebellar signs.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: MRI of the brain with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI)/ADC and posterior fossa/stroke protocol; magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) or computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the head and neck to evaluate the vertebrobasilar circulation; 12-lead ECG and cardiac telemetry; serum complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, coagulation studies, and lipid panel.
Conclusion: Central vertigo due to a right cerebellar/brainstem lesion, most likely a posterior circulation ischemic stroke. Urgent neuroimaging is required to confirm the diagnosis, exclude hemorrhage, and determine secondary prevention.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Neurology
Recommendations: 1) Immediate transfer to an emergency department for urgent evaluation and neuroimaging. 2) Obtain brain MRI with DWI/ADC as the first-line study; if MRI is unavailable, non-contrast CT head can screen for hemorrhage or mass effect but is insensitive for early posterior fossa ischemia. 3) Perform vascular imaging (MRA/CTA of head and neck) to assess for vertebrobasilar occlusion, stenosis, or arterial dissection. 4) Initiate cardiac monitoring and obtain an ECG to screen for atrial fibrillation or other cardioembolic sources. 5) Do not administer intravenous thrombolysis; the 5-day symptom duration places the patient well outside the therapeutic window. 6) If acute ischemic stroke is confirmed, initiate antiplatelet therapy and a high-intensity statin unless contraindicated. 7) Because this is a stroke in a young adult with vascular risk factors, pursue a full etiologic workup including evaluation for vertebral artery dissection, cardioembolism (telemetry, echocardiography), and thrombophilia if no clear source is identified. 8) Avoid aggressive blood pressure reduction unless markedly elevated; otherwise follow standard post-stroke blood pressure targets once the diagnosis is established. 9) Treat nausea/vomiting symptomatically, but avoid sedating vestibular suppressants that could mask neurological deterioration before imaging. 10) Obtain neurosurgical consultation if imaging reveals cerebellar edema, hemorrhage, or obstructive hydrocephalus.
Notes: The patient is outside the window for intravenous thrombolysis. Poster

Vignette:
A 19-year-old man presents with a 5-day history of severe sore throat that has progressively worsened despite 3 days of oral amoxicillin prescribed for pharyngitis. He now reports difficulty swallowing and has been unable to eat solid food for 2 days. He describes a muffled "hot potato" voice and difficulty fully opening his mouth. He has been drooling due to pain with swallowing. He denies respiratory difficulty. Vital signs show temperature 101.4°F, heart rate 98, blood pressure 124/78. On examination, there is trismus with limited mouth opening to approximately 2 cm. Intraoral exam reveals a bulging, erythematous soft palate on the left with displacement of the left tonsil medially and inferiorly. The uvula is deviated to the right. There is tender left anterior cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy. Lung auscultation is clear and there is no stridor.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 19-year-old
Sex: Male
Complaint: Severe progressive sore throat with difficulty swallowing solids, drooling, muffled "hot potato" voice, and difficulty opening the mouth, worsening despite 3 days of oral amoxicillin.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for a left peritonsillar abscess (quinsy). The strongest supporting facts are the combination of trismus with mouth opening limited to approximately 2 cm, a muffled "hot potato" voice, unilateral left soft palate bulging with medial and inferior displacement of the left tonsil, and uvular deviation to the right. These findings effectively separate this from uncomplicated exudative tonsillitis, which typically presents with bilateral tonsillar changes and lacks trismus, uvular deviation, or unilateral soft palate swelling. Epiglottitis is unlikely given the clear lung auscultation, absence of stridor or respiratory difficulty, and presence of intraoral lateralizing findings rather than supraglottic pathology. Retropharyngeal infection is less consistent with this age and the prominent intraoral unilateral bulging. Septic jugular thrombophlebitis is not supported by the localized peritonsillar examination and absence of antecedent severe unilateral neck pain or septic embolic signs. The drooling is attributable to odynophagia rather than airway obstruction.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Needle aspiration of the left peritonsillar space to confirm purulence and decompress the abscess; bedside equipment for incision and drainage and suction if needed.
Conclusion: Left peritonsillar abscess in a young adult with classic trismus, uvular deviation, and muffled voice, currently without airway compromise.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Proceed urgently with needle aspiration or incision and drainage of the left peritonsillar abscess. Initiate intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics active against oral flora and beta-lactamase producers (e.g., ceftriaxone plus metronidazole, or ampicillin-sulbactam) given failure of oral amoxicillin. Maintain nil per os until aspiration is performed and swallowing improves. Provide intravenous hydration, analgesia, and antiemetics as needed. Ensure airway monitoring and have advanced airway equipment readily available despite the current absence of respiratory difficulty; admit for observation if there is concern for airway compromise, dehydration, or inability to tolerate oral intake after drainage. If this is a recurrent episode, counsel regarding interval tonsillectomy after resolution; quinsy tonsillectomy may be considered if formal drainage fails or if abscess recurs. Send aspirated material for culture if feasible.
Notes: Continuously reassess for extension into the parapharyngeal space or descending deep neck infection.

He denies any history of atopic dermatitis, asthma, or food allergies. On examination, there are bilateral, symmetric, well-demarcated erythematous plaques on the dorsal hands with mild scaling. baseline_protocol:
Age: 28 years old
Sex: Female
Complaint: One-day history of nausea, three episodes of watery non-bloody diarrhea, and mild diffuse abdominal cramping.
Analysis: The presentation is most consistent with uncomplicated acute viral gastroenteritis. The strongest supporting facts are the sick contact (roommate with similar symptoms earlier in the week), acute onset of watery non-bloody stools without fever, and the patient’s ability to tolerate oral fluids with moist mucous membranes indicating adequate hydration. The physical examination shows only mild diffuse tenderness without guarding or rebound, arguing against peritoneal or surgical pathology. Main differential considerations include bacterial enteritis (less likely absent fever, bloody stool, or severe systemic symptoms), preformed toxin food poisoning (possible but typically explosive and very short-lived, and no shared suspect meal is reported), early appendicitis (unlikely given diffuse pain without migration to the right lower quadrant and absence of peritoneal signs), and inflammatory bowel disease (unlikely with a hyperacute one-day duration and no chronic history or bloody diarrhea). Stable vital signs and maintained oral intake confirm mild illness without significant dehydration.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Uncomplicated acute viral gastroenteritis with mild symptoms, stable hydration, and no red flags.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Continue oral rehydration with electrolyte-containing solutions and resume a normal light diet as tolerated (e.g., soups, crackers, rice, bananas). Use acetaminophen for cramping or discomfort if needed. Emphasize strict hand hygiene and disinfection of shared surfaces due to the likely contagious viral etiology in the household. Monitor urine output to ensure ongoing adequate hydration. Provide clear return precautions: seek immediate care if bloody stool, persistent vomiting, fever, severe or localized abdominal pain, dizziness, decreased urine output, or symptoms persisting or worsening beyond 48–72 hours develop.

On examination, there is tenderness and mild swelling over the radial styloid process and the first dorsal compartment. baseline_protocol:
Age: 32
Sex: Female
Complaint: 6-week progressive radial right wrist pain with difficulty gripping, turning the wrist, and making a fist, associated with repetitive infant lifting.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment (de Quervain's tenosynovitis). Strongest supporting facts include the postpartum status, repetitive lifting and holding motions, localized tenderness and mild swelling over the radial styloid and first dorsal compartment, a markedly positive Finkelstein test, reduced grip strength due to pain with preserved thumb range of motion, and normal wrist radiographs. The main differentials to exclude are first carpometacarpal arthritis (typically older, pain with axial loading/grind), intersection syndrome (more proximal forearm pain, crepitus), scaphoid injury (traumatic onset, anatomic snuffbox tenderness, radiographic abnormality), and superficial radial sensory nerve irritation (Wartenberg's syndrome, paresthesias, negative Finkelstein). The intact neurovascular examination and preserved thumb range of motion support a diagnosis of local tenosynovitis rather than articular or neurologic pathology.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Stenosing tenosynovitis (de Quervain's tenosynovitis) of the first dorsal compartment of the right wrist.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: 1) Activity modification and ergonomic adjustments for infant care to minimize repetitive thumb abduction and radial deviation. 2) Thumb spica splinting to rest the first dorsal compartment. 3) Ice and analgesia; confirm lactation status before prescribing systemic medications. 4) Consider referral for hand therapy for modalities and gentle stretching. 5) If symptoms persist after several weeks of conservative management, perform corticosteroid injection into the first dorsal compartment; ultrasound guidance is preferred to identify septation, ensure accurate placement, and improve outcomes. 6) Surgical release is indicated if conservative measures including injection fail.
Notes: A septated first dorsal compartment identified on ultrasound predicts higher failure rates with non-guided injection and may warrant ultrasound-guided injection or earlier surgical consideration. Confirm lactation status before pharmacologic therapy given the recent postpartum status.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.

Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. - If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Vignette:
A 62-year-old man with chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline GFR 22) on maintenance hemodialysis presents after missing his last two dialysis sessions due to transportation issues. He reports 2 days of progressive generalized weakness, muscle cramps, and palpitations. He has continued to eat his usual diet, including bananas and orange juice. On examination, he appears fatigued and mildly short of breath. Vital signs: T 36.6C, HR 52 (irregular), RR 20, BP 172/96, SpO2 95%. Lower extremity exam reveals 2+ bilateral pitting edema and diminished deep tendon reflexes. Labs: potassium 7.8 mEq/L, BUN 112 mg/dL, creatinine 11.4 mg/dL, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, phosphorus 8.2 mg/dL. ECG demonstrates absent P waves, widened QRS complexes (duration 180 ms), and peaked T waves with a sine wave pattern beginning to emerge. IV calcium gluconate is administered emergently.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 62 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Progressive generalized weakness, muscle cramps, palpitations, and missed maintenance hemodialysis sessions.
Analysis: The presentation is dominated by life-threatening severe hyperkalemia (potassium 7.8 mEq/L) causing pre-arrest cardiac toxicity. The ECG findings of absent P waves, widened QRS complex (180 ms), peaked T waves, and an emerging sine wave pattern are pathognomonic for critical hyperkalemia and indicate imminent risk of ventricular fibrillation or asystole. The patient missed two hemodialysis sessions and continued dietary potassium intake (bananas, orange juice), which are the strongest precipitating facts. Supporting evidence includes advanced renal failure (BUN 112 mg/dL, creatinine 11.4 mg/dL), severe metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate 14 mEq/L), hyperphosphatemia (8.2 mg/dL), and volume overload (2+ bilateral pitting edema, blood pressure 172/96, mild shortness of breath). Bradycardia (HR 52, irregular) and diminished deep tendon reflexes are consistent with severe electrolyte disturbance and uremia. Relevant differential considerations include uremic encephalopathy, hypocalcemia, hypermagnesemia, and acute hypervolemic pulmonary edema; however, the sine wave ECG makes hyperkalemic cardiotoxicity the immediate, overriding diagnosis requiring emergent intervention.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac monitoring; serial 12-lead ECGs; serial serum potassium testing.
Conclusion: Emergent, pre-arrest hyperkalemia (K+ 7.8 mEq/L) with sine wave ECG changes in a dialysis-dependent patient with missed sessions, complicated by uremia, metabolic acidosis, hyperphosphatemia, and volume overload.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Nephrology
Recommendations: 1) Maintain continuous cardiac telemetry with immediate defibrillation capability at bedside and obtain serial ECGs to monitor for arrhythmia progression or resolution. 2) Continue cardioprotection; consider repeat IV calcium gluconate if ECG changes persist after initial dose. 3) Initiate emergent hemodialysis immediately, as this is the definitive therapy for hyperkalemia, uremia, acidosis, hyperphosphatemia, and volume overload in this patient. 4) Administer temporizing, adjunctive potassium-shifting therapy while arranging dialysis: IV regular insulin with dextrose, nebulized beta-agonist therapy, and IV sodium bicarbonate given the severe metabolic acidosis. 5) Obtain ionized calcium and magnesium levels to guide further electrolyte management and avoid additional cardiac complications. 6) Restrict all oral potassium intake. 7) Admit to an intensive care setting for close monitoring until stabilized on dialysis. 8) Address transportation barriers and arrange social support to prevent future missed dialysis sessions.
Notes: The sine wave pattern indicates an imminent risk of cardiac arrest; all medical therapies listed are temporizing measures only and must not delay emergent dialysis.

Vignette:
A 15-year-old girl presents with her mother for evaluation of bumps on her forehead and chin that have been present for the past 3 months. She reports they are not painful but she finds them cosmetically bothersome. She has been washing her face with regular soap twice daily. She denies any cystic lesions, scarring, or use of new cosmetics. Menarche was 1 year ago and her cycles are regular. She takes no medications. On examination, there are scattered open and closed comedones on the forehead and chin numbering approximately 15 to 20. A few small inflammatory papules, each less than 5 mm, are noted on the chin. There are no nodules, cysts, or scarring.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 15-year-old
Sex: Female
Complaint: Bumps on the forehead and chin present for 3 months, cosmetically bothersome but not painful.
Analysis: The lesion count (~15–20 open and closed comedones with a few small inflammatory papules <5 mm) and the absence of nodules, cysts, or scarring classify this as mild acne vulgaris with a predominantly comedonal pattern and a mild inflammatory component, distinct from moderate inflammatory or severe nodulocystic disease. The forehead and chin distribution with visible comedones favors acne over perioral dermatitis (which typically lacks comedones and often involves perioral/orbital clusters), folliculitis (which usually presents with follicular pustules rather than comedones in this distribution), and keratosis pilaris (which presents with rough follicular papules on extensor surfaces rather than the face). Regular menses since menarche 1 year ago and lack of medication use reduce suspicion for hormonal or drug-induced causes. Regular soap may be contributing to irritation.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Mild acne vulgaris, predominantly comedonal with mild inflammatory papules, in an adolescent female.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Initiate topical retinoid therapy (e.g., adapalene or tretinoin) nightly for the comedonal component, with optional topical benzoyl peroxide (2.5%–5%) for the inflammatory papules. Replace regular soap with a gentle, non-comedogenic cleanser and moisturize; advise daily sunscreen, especially with retinoid use. Counsel that visible improvement typically requires 6–12 weeks of consistent use, with possible initial irritation. Given the absence of nodules, cysts, or scarring, systemic antibiotics, hormonal therapy, or isotretinoin are not indicated at this time. Schedule follow-up in 8–12 weeks to assess response and adjust therapy if needed.
Notes: None

Sex: Male

Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.

- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Vignette:
A 52-year-old woman with a 10-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with a 3-month history of progressively worsening stiffness and pain in her left shoulder. The pain is deep and aching, worse at night, and has made it increasingly difficult to reach behind her back, comb her hair, and fasten her bra. She denies any preceding trauma or injury. Her diabetes is managed with metformin and her last HbA1c was 7.8%. On examination, there is globally restricted active and passive range of motion of the left shoulder. External rotation is limited to 20 degrees (compared to 70 degrees on the right). Abduction is limited to 80 degrees, and internal rotation is severely restricted. There is no tenderness over specific rotator cuff tendons. Strength testing is limited by pain and stiffness. Shoulder radiographs show no fracture or dislocation and mild osteopenia.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 52
Sex: Female
Complaint: 3-month history of progressively worsening deep, aching left shoulder stiffness and pain, worse at night, causing difficulty reaching behind the back, combing hair, and fastening a bra; no preceding trauma.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder). The strongest supporting facts are: (1) type 2 diabetes mellitus (a major risk factor, with a recent HbA1c of 7.8%); (2) global restriction of both active and passive range of motion, with external rotation limited to 20° (vs 70° on the right) and abduction to 80°; (3) severe internal rotation restriction; (4) absence of specific rotator cuff tendon tenderness; and (5) shoulder radiographs showing no fracture, dislocation, or arthritic change. The equal limitation of active and passive motion distinguishes this from rotator cuff tendinopathy/tear, in which passive motion is typically preserved. Glenohumeral osteoarthritis is unlikely given the absence of radiographic joint space narrowing or osteophytes. Calcific tendinitis is less likely without radiographic calcification or focal tendon tenderness.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Left adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) in a 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, currently characterized by global active and passive motion restriction and night pain, without evidence of bony structural abnormality.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: 1) Perform baseline active and passive range-of-motion measurements in all planes to stage severity and establish objective metrics for tracking progress. 2) Initiate a graded, phase-matched nonoperative rehabilitation program: pendulum (Codman) exercises for early pain modulation and mobility; gentle passive stretching for external and internal rotation; wall-climbing/finger-walking for flexion and abduction; and joint mobilization techniques as tolerated. 3) Coordinate pain control timing with therapy sessions (e.g., heat before stretching, ice afterward, and alignment with prescribed analgesic timing) to maximize participation. 4) Counsel the patient that recovery often requires many months and that consistent daily home exercises are essential; diabetic patients may experience a more protracted course. 5) Recommend she discuss glycemic optimization with her physician, as an HbA1c of 7.8% is a modifiable factor that can worsen stiffness and prolong recovery. 6) If progress plateaus after 8–12 weeks of dedicated therapy, refer back to the physician for consideration of intra-articular corticosteroid injection or surgical release. 7) Provide adaptive strategies for activities of daily living during the painful phase.
Notes: Diabetic patients are at increased risk for bilateral adhesive capsulitis; the currently asymptomatic right shoulder should be monitored. Avoid aggressive, forceful passive stretching and high-velocity manipulation, particularly during the painful phase.

Vignette:
A 40-year-old man with a known history of chronic rhinosinusitis and bilateral nasal polyps presents with a 10-day history of worsening facial pressure, purulent nasal discharge, nasal congestion, and anosmia. He has had recurrent sinus infections averaging four to five times per year and has previously undergone polypectomy two years ago. He reports postnasal drip and a productive cough worse at night. He denies fever, visual changes, or severe headache. On examination, the nasal mucosa is edematous and erythematous bilaterally with visible polypoid tissue and mucopurulent drainage in the middle meatus. There is tenderness over the maxillary and frontal sinuses. Oropharynx shows cobblestoning of the posterior pharyngeal wall.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 40-year-old
Sex: Male
Complaint: 10-day worsening facial pressure, purulent nasal discharge, nasal congestion, anosmia, postnasal drip, and nocturnal productive cough in a patient with known chronic rhinosinusitis and bilateral nasal polyps.
Analysis: This presentation is most consistent with an acute bacterial exacerbation superimposed on chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP). The strongest supporting facts are the 10-day progressive course with purulent rhinorrhea, visible mucopurulent drainage in the middle meatus, facial pressure, and tenderness over the maxillary and frontal sinuses. The presence of bilateral polypoid tissue, recurrent sinus infections (four to five times per year), and prior polypectomy two years ago confirm underlying CRSwNP. Posterior pharyngeal cobblestoning reflects chronic postnasal drip. The absence of fever, visual changes, or severe headache argues against complicated sinusitis with orbital or intracranial involvement. Main differential considerations include acute viral rhinosinusitis (less likely given purulence, prior CRSwNP, and middle meatal drainage), allergic rhinitis exacerbation (typically presents with clear rhinorrhea and lacks facial pressure and purulence), and nonallergic rhinitis (does not explain purulence or sinus tenderness). Fixed structural obstruction from polyps contributes to baseline congestion but does not account for the acute purulent exacerbation.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: CT of the paranasal sinuses.
Conclusion: Acute bacterial exacerbation of chronic rhinosinusitis with bilateral nasal polyps in a patient with recurrent disease status post prior polypectomy, without features of complicated sinusitis.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Initiate empiric antibiotic therapy (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate) for 10–14 days for acute bacterial rhinosinusitis, with culture-directed modification if middle meatal purulence is sampled. Institute high-dose intranasal corticosteroid spray and high-volume saline irrigation to reduce mucosal edema and polyp inflammation. Consider a short oral corticosteroid burst for severe polyp-related obstruction and anosmia, with caution regarding metabolic risks of repeated courses. Obtain CT of the paranasal sinuses to define anatomic disease burden, ostiomeatal complex status, and exclude complications. Arrange ENT/rhinology follow-up to reassess the need for revision functional endoscopic sinus surgery if symptoms persist despite maximal medical therapy or if imaging demonstrates significant recurrent obstruction. Counsel the patient to seek emergent care immediately if fever, vision changes, severe headache, or periorbital swelling develop.
Notes: Monitor for emergent complications such as orbital or intracranial extension if severe headache, vision changes, or neurologic deficits develop.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 35-year-old
Sex: Male
Complaint: Progressive bilateral submandibular and sublingual swelling with worsening trismus, odynophagia, muffled "hot potato" voice, drooling, and respiratory distress following a recent lower left second molar extraction.
Analysis: The findings are classic for Ludwig's angina, a rapidly progressive, bilateral odontogenic infection involving the submandibular and sublingual spaces. The strongest supporting facts are the recent dental extraction; firm, woody, bilateral submandibular swelling with erythema and warmth; elevation and induration of the floor of the mouth with posterior and superior displacement of the tongue; inability to open the mouth; audible inspiratory stridor; and CT demonstration of multiloculated fluid collections with significant oropharyngeal airway narrowing. The patient is sitting upright and drooling, with an SpO2 of 91% on room air, indicating impending upper airway obstruction. Differential considerations include a localized submandibular abscess, parapharyngeal abscess, or peritonsillar abscess, but the bilateral, woody, brawny involvement of the floor of the mouth is most consistent with Ludwig's angina. Critically, the presence of trismus, tongue displacement, and stridor means standard laryngoscopy and bag-mask ventilation are unsafe.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A 35-year-old male with Ludwig's angina complicated by impending upper airway obstruction due to bilateral submandibular/sublingual space infection, tongue displacement, trismus, and significant oropharyngeal narrowing.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Manage the airway immediately in a controlled setting with an experienced team and a surgeon present. Keep the patient sitting upright and administer high-flow oxygen. Do not administer sedatives or neuromuscular blockade, as these can abolish the remaining airway tone and precipitate complete obstruction. Favor awake fiberoptic intubation performed by the most experienced operator. Prepare simultaneously for an elective surgical airway under local anesthesia if awake intubation is not feasible or fails. Ensure rigid bronchoscopy and an emergency surgical airway kit are immediately available as backup. After the airway is secured, proceed to urgent operative drainage with source control and initiate broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics. Admit to an intensive care unit for close monitoring.
Notes: None

Vignette:
A 24-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks gestation is brought in by ambulance after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home lasting approximately 2 minutes. Her partner reports she has complained of a persistent headache, visual disturbances described as flashing lights, and swelling of her face and hands over the past 2 days. She did not attend her last two prenatal appointments. On examination, she is postictal, moaning, and not following commands. Vital signs: T 37.6C, HR 112, RR 22, BP 182/116, SpO2 94%. Significant periorbital and bilateral upper extremity edema is present. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ bilaterally with sustained clonus at the ankles. Fetal heart rate monitoring shows persistent late decelerations. Labs: platelets 92,000/mcL, AST 286 U/L, ALT 312 U/L, LDH 680 U/L, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 5.2. IV magnesium sulfate is initiated and emergent cesarean delivery is planned.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 24 years old
Sex: Female
Complaint: Witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at 36 weeks gestation with persistent headache, flashing lights, facial and hand swelling, severe hypertension, and postictal altered mental status.
Analysis: The presentation is diagnostic of eclampsia complicating severe preeclampsia with features of HELLP syndrome (thrombocytopenia with platelets 92,000/mcL, elevated transaminases AST 286 U/L and ALT 312 U/L, elevated LDH 680 U/L), acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.4 mg/dL), and fetal compromise (persistent late decelerations). The strongest supporting facts include blood pressure 182/116 mmHg, sustained ankle clonus with 4+ deep tendon reflexes, significant proteinuria (urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 5.2), periorbital and upper extremity edema, and the recent seizure. Relevant differential considerations include intracranial hemorrhage from severe hypertension; however, the constellation of classic preeclamptic signs and laboratory abnormalities makes eclampsia the unifying diagnosis. From an anesthetic standpoint, the patient is postictal and not following commands, which contraindicates neuraxial anesthesia due to inability to cooperate and protect the airway, and the platelet count of 92,000/mcL in the setting of HELLP creates an unacceptably high risk of neuraxial hematoma with potential for rapid further decline. The fibrinogen level is not specified but is a critical determinant of coagulopathy and anesthetic choice.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Repeat complete blood count with platelet count; coagulation panel including PT/INR, aPTT, and fibrinogen; type and crossmatch for packed red blood cells.
Conclusion: A 24-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks with eclampsia, severe preeclampsia/HELLP syndrome, thrombocytopenia, and fetal distress requiring emergent cesarean delivery; anesthetic management is dominated by altered mental status, severe hypertension, and risk of evolving coagulopathy.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology
Recommendations: Proceed immediately to emergent cesarean delivery without delaying for neuroimaging. Favor rapid sequence general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation because the patient is postictal and not following commands, and because the platelet count is 92,000/mcL in the context of HELLP syndrome with risk of rapid decline; neuraxial anesthesia is contraindicated by mental status and the bleeding risk. Secure large-bore intravenous access and ensure immediate blood bank readiness. Continue IV magnesium sulfate with vigilant monitoring of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output to detect toxicity. Control severe hypertension prior to and during surgery, maintaining blood pressure below 160/110 mmHg with appropriate intravenous antihypertensive agents. Anticipate a potentially difficult airway due to significant periorbital and facial edema; have advanced airway equipment including video laryngoscopy and a smaller endotracheal tube immediately available. Maintain left uterine displacement and strict hemodynamic control during laryngoscopy and delivery. Obtain emergent repeat platelet count and coagulation studies including fibrinogen to assess for evolving consumptive coagulopathy before or concomitant with the procedure. Prepare for postpartum hemorrhage with immediate availability of packed red blood cells, fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate, and platelets. Coordinate with neonatology for immediate newborn resuscitation given persistent late decelerations and in-utero magnesium exposure. Plan postoperative management in an intensive care setting for ongoing blood pressure control, magnesium therapy, and laboratory monitoring.
Notes: Fibrinogen level is not specified in the case and must be checked emergently as it guides transfusion and anesthetic safety. Delivery should not be delayed for additional neuroimaging given the classic eclamptic presentation and fetal distress.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 16 years old
Sex: Female
Complaint: Mild right ankle pain after landing awkwardly on another player's foot during volleyball practice 2 hours ago.
Analysis: The presentation is most consistent with an isolated Grade I lateral ankle sprain of the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL). The strongest supporting facts are the mild localized tenderness over the ATFL with only mild lateral swelling and no ecchymosis; the ability to bear weight with minimal discomfort; and intact mechanical stability confirmed by negative anterior drawer and talar tilt tests. Non-tender bony landmarks and preserved weight-bearing effectively exclude a physeal or malleolar fracture. Main relevant differential considerations include: 1) Syndesmotic (high) ankle sprain—unlikely given the mechanism and isolated lateral symptoms without proximal tenderness; 2) Peroneal tendon injury—less likely because tenderness is directly over the ATFL rather than posterior to the lateral malleolus; and 3) Ankle fracture—effectively ruled out by non-tender bony landmarks and full weight-bearing capacity.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Acute Grade I lateral ankle sprain (ATFL) with stable ankle mechanics and no evidence of fracture or syndesmotic involvement in a competitive volleyball player.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Initiate functional rehabilitation with a lace-up or semi-rigid ankle brace for support during ambulation and sports. Continue progressive weight-bearing as tolerated; crutches are unnecessary. Apply intermittent ice and compression for the first 24–48 hours. Begin early range-of-motion exercises (e.g., ankle circles, alphabet exercises, dorsiflexion/plantarflexion) within pain limits. Progress to resisted strengthening of the peroneals and calves, then to single-leg balance and proprioception drills on stable and unstable surfaces. Advance to sport-specific training, including jumping, hopping, cutting, and controlled landing mechanics, once pain-free with full range of motion and near-normal strength. Implement a stepwise return-to-sport plan: pain-free practice → restricted drills → full volleyball participation, maintaining bracing during the initial return. Emphasize proper landing mechanics and neuromuscular training to reduce recurrence risk.
Notes: None

A 34-year-old woman with no known underlying lung disease 12-day history of cough. She initially had nasal congestion and a mild sore throat, but now her symptoms are all related to a productive cough without paroxysms. She denies any sick contacts. baseline_protocol:
Age: 34 years old
Sex: Female
Complaint: 12-day productive cough with diffuse wheezing following a recent upper respiratory illness.
Analysis: The presentation is consistent with acute bronchitis developing after a viral upper respiratory infection, supported by the antecedent nasal congestion and sore throat. She is afebrile with normal vital signs and no respiratory distress, making pneumonia unlikely. The diffuse scattered wheezes indicate acute bronchospasm. She has no known underlying lung disease, which argues against pre-existing asthma or prior wheezing episodes. The lack of paroxysmal cough reduces concern for pertussis. The primary distinction is between transient post-infectious bronchial hyperreactivity and newly unmasked or underlying asthma; the clinical context favors a transient process, with the response to a bronchodilator trial serving as the next discriminatory step.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Bronchodilator trial (e.g., albuterol via metered-dose inhaler with spacer) to assess reversibility of bronchospasm and wheeze.
Conclusion: Acute bronchitis with transient bronchial hyperreactivity and diffuse bronchospasm in the setting of a resolving viral upper respiratory tract infection.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology
Recommendations: Initiate an inhaled short-acting bronchodilator (e.g., albuterol) for symptomatic relief of wheeze and bronchospasm. Counsel that this presentation most likely represents transient post-infectious airway hyperreactivity rather than asthma, given the recent URI and lack of prior lung disease. Provide supportive care and avoid antibiotics in the absence of bacterial infection indicators. Set a clear threshold for follow-up: if wheeze or cough persists after the acute illness resolves, obtain spirometry and arrange pulmonology follow-up to evaluate for underlying asthma.
Notes: None

Vignette:
A 24-year-old man presents with a painful small bump in his beard area that appeared 2 days after shaving. He shaves with a multi-blade razor and shaves against the grain. He denies fever, spreading redness, or drainage. He has no history of recurrent skin infections. On examination, there is a single erythematous, firm papule approximately 4 mm in diameter on the right submandibular area. Mild swelling is present around the lesion. A curled hair is visible beneath the surface of the skin. There is no fluctuance, induration, or streaking erythema.

Sex: Male
Complaint: Painful small bump in the beard area that appeared 2 days after shaving.

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.

Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.

- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 28
Sex: Female
Complaint: Sudden onset severe left-sided pelvic pain and lightheadedness in a pregnant woman with 7 weeks of amenorrhea.
Analysis: The patient is in hemorrhagic shock manifested by hypotension (78/48 mmHg), tachycardia (132 bpm), tachypnea (24), pallor, diaphoresis, and anemia (hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL). The combination of amenorrhea, a positive pregnancy test, an empty uterus on bedside transvaginal ultrasound, a complex left adnexal mass with ring-of-fire sign, and significant free fluid in the pelvis and Morison’s pouch confirms a ruptured left tubal ectopic pregnancy with massive hemoperitoneum. Cervical motion tenderness, peritoneal signs, and a tender left adnexal mass on examination further support rupture. Risk factors explicitly present include prior pelvic inflammatory disease and a prior left tubal ectopic pregnancy treated with methotrexate, indicating recurrent ipsilateral disease. Differential considerations include ruptured corpus luteum cyst with hemorrhage, heterotopic pregnancy, or septic abortion, but the clinical and sonographic findings overwhelmingly point to ruptured ectopic pregnancy causing hemodynamic collapse.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Ruptured left tubal ectopic pregnancy with hemoperitoneum and hemorrhagic shock requiring immediate surgical hemostasis.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology
Recommendations: Proceed immediately to the operating room for emergent laparotomy without awaiting further studies. Initiate massive transfusion with O-negative blood and blood products, coordinated with anesthesia and the blood bank, while continuing aggressive resuscitation. Evacuate hemoperitoneum and perform left salpingectomy or salpingostomy to achieve definitive hemostasis. Given the history of prior left tubal ectopic disease and current hemodynamic instability, prioritize life-saving hemorrhage control; salpingectomy is appropriate if the tube is not salvageable or hemostasis is tenuous. Postoperatively, admit to a monitored setting, serially monitor quantitative beta-hCG to resolution, and counsel the patient regarding future ectopic recurrence risk and fertility implications once clinically stabilized.
Notes: None

Vignette:
A 42-year-old man presents with mild low back ache that developed after spending several hours gardening yesterday. He was bending and lifting bags of soil. The pain is localized to the lower back and does not radiate to the legs. He denies numbness, tingling, weakness, or changes in bowel or bladder function. He has no history of prior back surgery or chronic back problems. On examination, there is mild paraspinal muscle tenderness in the lumbar region bilaterally. Range of motion is mildly reduced on flexion. Straight leg raise is negative bilaterally. Neurological examination of the lower extremities is normal.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 42
Sex: Male
Complaint: Mild low back ache localized to the lower back after several hours of gardening involving bending and lifting bags of soil; no radiation to the legs and no neurological symptoms.
Analysis: The presentation is most consistent with acute mechanical low back pain (lumbar paraspinal muscle strain) precipitated by repetitive bending and lifting. The strongest supporting facts are the clear post-exertional onset during gardening, localized non-radiating pain, bilateral paraspinal tenderness, mildly reduced lumbar flexion, negative straight leg raise bilaterally, and a completely normal lower extremity neurological examination. The absence of red flags—specifically no prior back surgery, no chronic back problems, and no bowel or bladder dysfunction, numbness, tingling, or weakness—makes serious underlying pathology unlikely. Main relevant differential considerations include lumbar muscle strain/sprain, mechanical low back pain, and discogenic or facet-mediated pain without radiculopathy; cauda equina syndrome, fracture, infection, and malignancy are not supported by the history or examination.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Acute mechanical low back pain/lumbar strain secondary to repetitive lifting and bending during gardening; benign condition without red flags or neurological deficit, expected to recover over days to weeks with conservative management.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: 1) Activity modification: Maintain light daily activity and walking as tolerated; avoid prolonged bed rest and temporarily refrain from heavy lifting, sustained bending, and repetitive gardening tasks. 2) Body mechanics and ergonomics: Teach proper lifting technique (hip hinge, neutral spine, keep loads close to the body) and gardening positioning (half-kneeling, avoid sustained flexion, take frequent breaks, consider raised beds or knee pads). 3) Graded exercise program: Initiate gentle stretching for lumbar paraspinals, hip flexors, and hamstrings; progress to core stabilization exercises (e.g., pelvic tilts, dead bug, bird dog, modified planks) as pain allows. 4) Symptom management: Apply superficial heat or ice to the lumbar region as tolerated; short-term over-the-counter analgesics may be used if not contraindicated and in coordination with a primary care provider. 5) Gradual return to activity: Progressively reintroduce gardening and household tasks over days to weeks as symptoms improve. 6) Expectation setting and precautions: Anticipate resolution within days to several weeks; return promptly for reassessment if pain radiates, numbness/tingling develops, weakness occurs, or bowel/bladder symptoms emerge. 7) Follow-up: Re-evaluate in 1–2 weeks to assess lumbar range of motion, paraspinal tenderness, and core/hip strength, and to advance the exercise program.
Notes: None

Sex: Man

Vignette:
A 22-year-old female soccer player presents to the sports medicine clinic two days after sustaining a left knee injury during a game. She reports that while pivoting to change direction she felt a sudden pop in her knee followed by immediate swelling and inability to continue playing. She was unable to bear full weight and has been using crutches since. She denies any prior knee injuries. On examination, there is a moderate effusion of the left knee. Range of motion is limited by pain and swelling. The Lachman test is positive with a soft endpoint on the left, and the anterior drawer test demonstrates increased anterior tibial translation compared to the right. McMurray test is equivocal. The collateral ligaments are stable. She is neurovascularly intact distally.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 22
Sex: Female
Complaint: Acute left knee injury sustained while pivoting during soccer, characterized by a sudden pop, immediate swelling, inability to bear weight, and persistent pain and instability.
Analysis: The presentation is highly consistent with an acute anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear. The pivoting mechanism, audible pop, and immediate swelling are classic historical features for ACL rupture. The moderate effusion and limited range of motion support an acute traumatic intra-articular process. The positive Lachman test with a soft endpoint and increased anterior tibial translation on the anterior drawer test are the strongest objective evidence of ACL disruption. Stable collateral ligaments make a multi-ligament knee injury less likely. The equivocal McMurray test does not exclude an associated meniscal tear, which commonly accompanies ACL injuries. While an isolated meniscal injury or osteochondral lesion remains in the differential, the full constellation of findings most strongly supports an ACL tear.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Plain radiographs (AP and lateral) of the left knee to exclude fracture or avulsion; magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the left knee to confirm ACL integrity and evaluate for associated meniscal, chondral, or other ligamentous injuries.
Conclusion: Acute left anterior cruciate ligament tear with traumatic knee effusion, likely isolated given stable collateral ligaments, with possible associated intra-articular pathology not yet excluded.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Continue protected weight bearing with crutches and use a hinged knee brace or immobilizer. Initiate RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation) and appropriate analgesia. Arrange urgent referral to orthopedics or sports medicine for definitive evaluation and management planning. Obtain left knee radiographs and MRI. Begin early gentle range-of-motion and quadriceps activation exercises as pain allows to prevent stiffness and atrophy. Strictly avoid pivoting, cutting, jumping, or return to sport until cleared by a specialist. Given the patient’s age and activity level as a soccer player, discuss the prognosis and potential for surgical ACL reconstruction following imaging and specialist assessment. Explicitly address the equivocal McMurray test by having MRI assess for concurrent meniscal pathology and by monitoring for mechanical symptoms.
Notes: None

Vignette: A 6-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician by his mother who noticed patches of hair loss on his scalp over the past 3 weeks. The patches have been gradually enlarging and the affected areas appear scaly. He attends elementary school and his mother reports several classmates have had similar issues. Vignette:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician by his mother who noticed patches of hair loss on his scalp over the past 3 weeks. The patches have been gradually enlarging and the affected areas appear scaly. He attends elementary school and his mother reports several classmates have had similar issues. He denies pain but admits to mild itching. On examination, there are two well-defined round patches of alopecia on the parietal and occipital scalp, measuring approximately 3 cm and 2 cm in diameter respectively. Within the patches, the hair shafts are broken off at the surface giving a black-dot appearance. The surrounding scalp is covered with fine gray-white scale. There is mild posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. A Wood lamp examination reveals no fluorescence. KOH preparation of plucked hairs shows endothrix spores surrounding and within the hair shaft.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 6 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Progressive scaly patches of hair loss on the scalp with mild itching over 3 weeks.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for tinea capitis. The strongest supporting facts are the well-defined round patches of alopecia with fine gray-white scale, the black-dot appearance from hairs broken off at the surface, mild posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, a history of classmates with similar issues, and a positive KOH preparation demonstrating endothrix spores surrounding and within the hair shafts. The absence of Wood lamp fluorescence is consistent with an endothrix pattern. The main differential considerations include alopecia areata (usually lacks scale and broken black-dot hairs), trichotillomania (typically shows irregular patches with hairs of varying length and no significant scale), and seborrheic dermatitis (diffuse scaling without well-demarcated alopecia); however, the combination of clinical morphology and confirmed fungal elements makes tinea capitis the clear diagnosis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Tinea capitis (endothrix dermatophyte infection of the scalp).
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Initiate systemic oral antifungal therapy (standard pediatric first-line regimen, e.g., griseofulvin or terbinafine), as topical agents alone cannot penetrate the hair shaft to achieve cure. Use an adjunctive antifungal shampoo (e.g., selenium sulfide or ketoconazole) twice weekly to reduce spore shedding and carriage. School exclusion is unnecessary once treatment has begun; advise the family to inform the school or parents of affected classmates so other children can be evaluated. Instruct the family to avoid sharing combs, hats, pillows, or other hair accessories, and screen household contacts for scaling or hair loss. Arrange follow-up in 4–8 weeks to assess clinical response and hair regrowth.
Notes: Endothrix infections typically do not fluoresce under Wood lamp examination, and cosmetic hair regrowth may lag behind clinical clearance by several weeks to months.
