criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 14-year-old boy with no significant past medical history presents 3 days after developing a red, irritated right eye that spread to the left eye today. He has watery discharge from both eyes and they are stuck shut in the morning. He reports recent upper respiratory symptoms and that several children at his day camp recently had pink eye. He denies significant pain or light sensitivity and does not wear contact lenses. On examination, his pupils are equal and reactive and he has a right-sided, tender preauricular lymph node. Penlight examination does not reveal any corneal opacity
baseline_protocol:
Age: 14-year-old
Sex: Male
Complaint: Three days of bilateral red, irritated eyes with watery discharge and morning crusting, spreading from the right to the left eye, following recent upper respiratory symptoms and exposure to other children with conjunctivitis at day camp.
Analysis: The presentation is most consistent with acute viral conjunctivitis, likely adenoviral (pharyngoconjunctival fever). The strongest supporting facts are the watery (non-purulent) discharge, progression from one eye to the other via autoinoculation, associated upper respiratory symptoms, documented outbreak exposure at day camp, and the presence of a tender right preauricular lymph node. The absence of significant pain, photophobia, or corneal opacity on penlight examination makes herpetic keratitis, corneal ulceration, and anterior uveitis unlikely. Bacterial conjunctivitis is less favored because the discharge is watery rather than purulent and because preauricular adenopathy is atypical. Allergic conjunctivitis is unlikely given the contagious exposure, morning crusting, and lack of prominent pruritus. The fact that the patient does not wear contact lenses reduces concern for Pseudomonas or Acanthamoeba keratitis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Acute viral conjunctivitis, most likely adenoviral and outbreak-related, in a 14-year-old male without evidence of corneal involvement or bacterial superinfection.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology
Recommendations: Initiate supportive care with preservative-free artificial tears and cool compresses for comfort. Instruct the patient and household on strict hand hygiene, avoidance of eye rubbing, and no sharing of towels, pillows, or eye cosmetics. Gently cleanse dried discharge from the eyelid margins with warm water. Counsel that viral conjunctivitis is highly contagious; advise temporary exclusion from day camp until eyes are no longer actively draining or per camp policy, and notify camp administration of the outbreak to reinforce hand and surface hygiene measures. Do not prescribe topical antibiotics. Schedule follow-up if symptoms worsen or fail to improve within 5 to 7 days. Advise the family to seek urgent re-evaluation immediately if the patient develops eye pain, photophobia, decreased vision, or any corneal opacity.
Notes: Tender preauricular lymphadenopathy strongly supports a viral etiology but is not pathognomonic; the emergence of pain, photophobia, or visual changes would require urgent slit-lamp examination to exclude herpetic or other corneal disease.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 18 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Severe headache, fever, photophobia, and neck stiffness.
Analysis: The patient is an 18-year-old male with a 3-day history of severe headache and fever, with examination findings of photophobia and neck stiffness. These features constitute the classic triad for meningitis with associated meningeal irritation. The primary diagnostic consideration is acute meningitis, which may be bacterial or viral. Subarachnoid hemorrhage is less likely given the presence of fever and the subacute course over three days, but should be considered in the differential of severe headache. No focal neurological deficits are described, yet this does not exclude serious central nervous system infection. The presentation warrants urgent neuroimaging and cerebrospinal fluid evaluation to confirm the diagnosis and guide therapy.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Noncontrast head CT to evaluate for mass effect, intracranial hemorrhage, or contraindications to lumbar puncture; lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid analysis (cell count with differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, bacterial culture, and viral PCR as indicated); blood cultures.
Conclusion: Acute meningitis is the leading diagnosis in this 18-year-old male presenting with fever, severe headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness; this is a neurological emergency requiring immediate evaluation and empiric treatment.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Neurology
Recommendations: Obtain emergent noncontrast head CT to assess for mass effect, hemorrhage, or other contraindications to lumbar puncture. Perform lumbar puncture with CSF studies and obtain blood cultures. Initiate empiric antimicrobial therapy immediately if bacterial meningitis is suspected; do not delay antibiotics for imaging or LP if the patient is unstable or if significant delays are anticipated. Monitor closely for altered mental status, seizures, or signs of increased intracranial pressure. Additional considerations include the high risk of morbidity and mortality from bacterial meningitis in young adults, the possibility of a partially treated infection, and the need for appropriate infection control precautions pending definitive diagnosis.
Notes: Noncontrast head CT may be normal in early meningitis and does not exclude the diagnosis; clinical suspicion and CSF analysis must guide management.

Consider a 40-year-old, monogamous, married woman who calls to report a 2-day history of vaginal itching and thick white discharge. She has no abdominal pain or fever. (in study 50% recommended physician visit)
baseline_protocol:
Age: 40-year-old
Sex: Female
Complaint: 2-day history of vaginal itching and thick white discharge; no abdominal pain or fever.
Analysis: The acute onset of vulvar pruritus with thick white discharge is most consistent with uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis. The absence of abdominal pain, fever, and malodorous discharge makes bacterial vaginosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and complicated infection unlikely. Trichomoniasis is less probable given the thick white character of the discharge and her monogamous relationship. Contact dermatitis or irritant vulvopathy may cause itching but typically do not produce thick discharge. Pelvic examination with microscopy is needed to confirm fungal elements before or alongside treatment.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Pelvic examination with speculum; vaginal pH testing; saline wet mount and/or 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) microscopy of vaginal discharge.
Conclusion: Presumed acute uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis, pending confirmatory microscopic examination.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology
Recommendations: Schedule an outpatient gynecology visit for pelvic examination and office microscopy. If budding yeast or pseudohyphae are identified, initiate antifungal therapy (e.g., topical intravaginal azole or single-dose oral fluconazole 150 mg if not pregnant). Advise against douching and use of intravaginal irritants. Counsel that partner treatment is not indicated for candidiasis. If infections are recurrent, evaluate for diabetes or immunosuppression.

Subclinical specialization: Cardiology

Initiate aspirin therapy and a high-intensity statin unless contraindicated. Prescribe sublingual nitroglycerin for breakthrough chest pain with explicit counseling that nitrates are absolutely contraindicated within 24 hours of sildenafil use due to risk of severe hypotension. Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.

This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

Vignette:
A 67-year-old woman with a history of COPD presents with 3 days of worsening dyspnea and increased frequency of coughing. Her cough is now productive of green, purulent sputum. The patient has a 100-pack-year history of smoking. She has had intermittent, low-grade fever of 100°F (37.7°C) for the past 3 days and her appetite is poor. baseline_protocol:
Age: 67
Sex: Female
Complaint: Worsening dyspnea and productive cough with green, purulent sputum over 3 days, accompanied by low-grade fever, poor appetite, and increased rescue bronchodilator use in a patient with known COPD.
Analysis: The presentation is most consistent with an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD), likely triggered by a bacterial respiratory infection. The strongest supporting facts are the established COPD diagnosis, 100-pack-year smoking history, progressive dyspnea beyond baseline, increased cough frequency, purulent sputum, low-grade fever, and the need for increased rescue inhaler use. The triad of increased dyspnea, sputum volume, and purulence supports empiric antibiotic therapy. The main differential considerations include community-acquired pneumonia, which must be excluded with imaging, and a viral respiratory infection; less likely is an isolated cardiac event given the purulent sputum and fever. Given the risk of respiratory failure and the severity of symptoms, inpatient management is warranted.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Chest radiography; pulse oximetry; arterial or venous blood gas; complete blood count; basic metabolic panel; sputum Gram stain and culture; blood cultures; electrocardiogram.
Conclusion: Acute exacerbation of COPD, likely bacterial in etiology, requiring inpatient management with oxygen, bronchodilators, corticosteroids, empiric antibiotics, and close respiratory monitoring while excluding pneumonia.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology
Recommendations: 1) Admit for inpatient monitoring and reconcile home medications, continuing maintenance bronchodilators unless contraindicated. 2) Administer supplemental oxygen titrated to maintain SpO2 88–92% to avoid precipitating hypercapnic respiratory failure. 3) Initiate frequent short-acting inhaled bronchodilator therapy with both a beta-agonist and an anticholinergic. 4) Start systemic corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone 40 mg orally daily or an IV equivalent). 5) Initiate empiric antibiotics targeting typical respiratory pathogens given the presence of purulence, increased sputum, and worsening dyspnea. 6) Obtain chest radiography promptly to rule out concomitant pneumonia. 7) Obtain blood gas analysis to assess for hypoxemia and/or hypercapnia. 8) Initiate pharmacologic venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. 9) If hypercapnic respiratory failure or acidosis develops, escalate to non-invasive positive pressure ventilation. 10) Provide smoking cessation counseling and assess age-appropriate respiratory vaccinations prior to discharge.
Notes: Avoid uncontrolled high-concentration oxygen therapy because of the risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure in patients with underlying COPD.

Vignette: A 44-year-old woman presents with a 1-year history of persistent redness across her cheeks, nose, and chin that has gradually worsened. She reports frequent flushing triggered by hot beverages, spicy food, and emotional stress. Over the past 3 months she has developed scattered small red bumps and occasional pustules on her cheeks. She reports a stinging and burning sensation with many topical products. She denies eye symptoms. She has fair skin and a family history of rosacea in her mother. Vignette:
A 44-year-old woman presents with a 1-year history of persistent redness across her cheeks, nose, and chin that has gradually worsened. She reports frequent flushing triggered by hot beverages, spicy food, and emotional stress. Over the past 3 months she has developed scattered small red bumps and occasional pustules on her cheeks. She reports a stinging and burning sensation with many topical products. She denies eye symptoms. She has fair skin and a family history of rosacea in her mother. On examination, there is diffuse centrofacial erythema with multiple visible telangiectasias across the cheeks and nasal bridge. Several 2 to 3 mm inflammatory papules and scattered pustules are present on the cheeks bilaterally. There are no comedones. The skin of the forehead and perioral area is relatively spared.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 44
Sex: Female
Complaint: Persistent centrofacial redness with flushing, visible facial blood vessels, and recent onset of small inflammatory bumps and pustules on the cheeks, accompanied by stinging and burning sensitivity to topical products.
Analysis: The clinical picture is most consistent with rosacea, with overlapping erythematotelangiectatic and papulopustular features. The strongest supporting facts are the centrofacial distribution (cheeks, nose, chin) with relative sparing of the forehead and perioral area; trigger-induced flushing from hot beverages, spicy food, and emotional stress; the presence of telangiectasias; inflammatory papules and pustules without comedones; skin sensitivity and burning to topical products; fair skin; and a first-degree family history of rosacea. The absence of comedones makes acne vulgaris unlikely. Seborrheic dermatitis is less likely given the lack of greasy scaling in typical areas. Cutaneous lupus erythematosus is unlikely because the lesions include papulopustules and telangiectasias without associated systemic signs, scarring, or photosensitive poikiloderma. Demodicosis can present similarly but the combination of flushing triggers, chronic centrofacial erythema, and telangiectasias favors rosacea.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Papulopustular rosacea with erythematotelangiectatic features in a 44-year-old fair-skinned woman.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: 
1. Skin care modification: Immediately discontinue all topical products that cause stinging or burning. Use a mild, non-soap cleanser with lukewarm (not hot) water only. Apply a gentle, fragrance-free, non-comedogenic moisturizer and a physical broad-spectrum sunscreen daily to accommodate fair, sensitive skin and minimize flushing.
2. Trigger avoidance: Avoid identified triggers including hot beverages, spicy foods, and emotional stress where possible; minimize exposure to heat, saunas, and sudden temperature changes.
3. Topical pharmacotherapy: Initiate topical metronidazole, azelaic acid, or ivermectin for the inflammatory papules and pustules; consider topical brimonidine or oxymetazoline for persistent background facial erythema under clinician guidance.
4. Systemic therapy: If papulopustular inflammation is moderate or refractory, a course of subantimicrobial-dose oral doxycycline may be considered by the prescribing clinician.
5. Vascular treatment: Refer to dermatology for evaluation of pulsed dye laser or intense pulsed light therapy to address telangiectasias once active papulopustular inflammation is controlled.
6. Monitoring and follow-up: Although eye symptoms are currently denied, screen for ocular rosacea at each visit. Review adherence, skin tolerance, and treatment response in 8–12 weeks, adjusting the regimen based on sensitivity and efficacy.
Notes: None

criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 2-yr-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of a 1-day
history of cough and difficulty breathing. The parents state that the boy appeared normal until
the previous night when he began coughing shortly after dinner. The cough stopped after about
an hour; the child felt better and went to bed. In the morning, the cough returned and he began
to have difficulty breathing, which the parents think is worsening. No one else at home is ill.

Review of Systems:
General: The child has no fever or malaise, and he was well until the cough began.

Skin: No rash is noted.

HEENT: He does not have sore throat, runny nose, ear pain, difficulty swallowing, or eye
discharge or redness.

Pulmonary: The child has been coughing and is short of breath.

Cardiovascular: The child has not had chest pain.

Gastrointestinal: The child has not had abdominal pain, vomiting, or diarrhea. The parents say
he did not want to eat breakfast because of the cough and dyspnea.

Genitourinary: Noncontributory

Musculoskeletal: Noncontributory

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Full-term, normal delivery. The boy has been healthy since birth except for two
episodes of wheezing; each required a short course of bronchodilators but no daily treatment.

Surgical history: None

Medications: None

Allergies: None

Family history: Mother has mild, well-controlled asthma; father is healthy.

Social history: The child lives with his mother, father, and pet dog. The child's vaccinations
are up to date.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Well-developed male child, awake and alert, who has obvious dry cough
and mild respiratory distress. No cyanosis. He is able to speak with a normal-sounding voice.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37° C
Pulse: 115 beats/min
BP: 100/75 mm Hg
Respirations: 30/min

Skin: Pink, warm, dry; no cyanosis or rash. Capillary refill normal.

HEENT: Tympanic membranes normal bilaterally. Nasal passages clear, no discharge. No
drooling. No erythema or exudate in pharynx. Nontender, supple neck; no adenopathy.

Pulmonary: Significant wheezing in the left lung that appears to be transmitted to the right lung.
No rhonchi, rales, or stridor; no retractions or use of accessory muscles.

Cardiovascular: Mild tachycardia. S1 and S2 normal; no murmurs rubs or gallops.

Gastrointestinal: Abdomen soft and not tender or distended. Bowel sounds normal.

Genitourinary: Unremarkable

Musculoskeletal: Normal appearance and movement of extremities.

Neurologic: Awake and alert. Cranial nerves grossly intact. Normal motor and sensory exam.

Mental status: Responds appropriately for his age.

Results of appropriate testing return and show the following:
● Pulse oximetry: 96% on room air.
● Chest x-ray: Report states "AP and lateral views normal. The child is unable to
cooperate with expiratory view."

Test results: Chest x-ray in the left and right lateral decubitus positions are taken and shown.

Age: 2 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Acute onset cough and difficulty breathing beginning shortly after dinner, with asymmetric left-sided wheezing.
Analysis: In a toddler, the sudden onset of cough and dyspnea temporally related to eating, combined with localized left lung wheezing and a normal AP/lateral chest radiograph, is highly suggestive of foreign body aspiration into the left main bronchus. Decubitus chest radiographs were appropriately obtained to assess for positional air trapping, an adjunctive finding in bronchial obstruction. The child is afebrile, lacks upper respiratory or systemic infectious symptoms, and is hemodynamically stable with adequate oxygenation, making viral bronchiolitis or pneumonia less likely. While the child has a history of prior wheezing and maternal asthma, the acute focal presentation after a meal and the need for decubitus views point toward an obstructing bronchial foreign body rather than an isolated asthma exacerbation.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Rigid bronchoscopy
Conclusion: Suspected left bronchial foreign body aspiration causing partial airway obstruction; patient is currently stable without respiratory failure.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Urgent ENT consultation for rigid bronchoscopy to directly visualize the airway and remove the suspected foreign body. Maintain NPO status. Provide continuous pulse oximetry and cardiorespiratory monitoring. Keep pediatric airway resuscitation equipment immediately available. Avoid further imaging or delays that could postpone definitive airway management. Administer supplemental oxygen if saturation declines. Counsel the family that radiolucent foreign bodies are often not visible on plain radiographs and that bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

She reports her menstrual periods have been heavy for the past year with cycles lasting 7 to 8 days and requiring frequent pad changes. She has also noticed brittle nails and a craving for ice. baseline_protocol:
Age: 25 years old
Sex: Male
Complaint: Collapse during outdoor training in hot, humid conditions with altered mental status, hyperthermia, and hemodynamic instability.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for exertional heat stroke (EHS) precipitated by high ambient temperature (102°F), high humidity (85%), strenuous activity with full gear, and inadequate hydration. The strongest supporting facts include a core temperature of 41.1°C (106°F), central nervous system dysfunction (GCS 8, intermittent decorticate posturing), anhidrosis with hot dry skin, and hemodynamic collapse (blood pressure 86/52, heart rate 148). Laboratory evidence confirms severe multi-organ injury: rhabdomyolysis (CK 12,400 U/L), acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.6 mg/dL), hepatic transaminitis (AST 482 U/L, ALT 326 U/L), coagulopathy (INR 1.6, platelets 98,000/mcL), severe hypernatremia (152 mEq/L), hyperkalemia (5.8 mEq/L), and lactic acidosis (7.2 mmol/L). Relevant differential considerations include sepsis/septic shock, malignant hyperthermia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, serotonin syndrome, and thyrotoxicosis; however, the environmental context, exertional history, and thermoregulatory failure make EHS the unifying diagnosis, with progression to multi-organ dysfunction.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous core temperature monitoring (rectal or esophageal probe), 12-lead ECG to evaluate for hyperkalemia-induced changes, arterial blood gas, urinalysis for myoglobin, fibrinogen and D-dimer to assess for disseminated intravascular coagulation, and type and screen.
Conclusion: Exertional heat stroke with severe multi-organ dysfunction manifesting as rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, hepatic injury, coagulopathy with thrombocytopenia, hypernatremia, hyperkalemia, and encephalopathy.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: 1) Continue aggressive active cooling (cold water immersion, ice packs to axillae/groin, cold IV saline) with a goal to reduce core temperature below 39°C within 30 minutes; stop cooling at approximately 38°C to avoid hypothermia. 2) Administer aggressive isotonic crystalloid resuscitation for hemodynamic support. 3) Obtain a 12-lead ECG immediately and treat hyperkalemia with standard measures (calcium, insulin/glucose, beta-agonists) if ECG changes are present; given creatinine 2.6 mg/dL and CK 12,400 U/L, initiate urgent nephrology consultation for renal replacement therapy. 4) Use benzodiazepines for shivering suppression and seizure prophylaxis. 5) Admit to the intensive care unit for continuous cardiac and core temperature monitoring. 6) Monitor for and treat compartment syndrome given massive rhabdomyolysis; maintain urine output greater than 0.5 mL/kg/hr if hemodynamically feasible. 7) Transfuse blood products only if active bleeding or before invasive procedures given existing coagulopathy. 8) Repeat CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation studies, CK, and lactate every 4 to 6 hours to track organ function and DIC progression. 9) Do not administer antipyretics (acetaminophen or NSAIDs) or dantrolene, as they are ineffective in heat stroke.
Notes: Antipyretics and dantrolene are contraindicated and ineffective in environmental and exertional heat stroke.

criterion:

Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
An 80-yr-old woman is brought to the emergency department by emergency medical services
(EMS) personnel because of a syncopal episode at home. She had been in the shower,
suddenly felt weak, and collapsed to the floor. Her husband heard her fall and found her awake,
lying on the bathroom floor. He called EMS who, when they arrived in the patient's home,
found her to be tachycardic and hypotensive. On arrival in the emergency department, she is
confused and has difficulty answering questions. Her husband states she has hypertension,
dyslipidemia, and mild dementia and, 1 wk ago, had a transcatheter aortic valve replacement for
severe aortic stenosis. He was told the procedure had been uncomplicated and states that his
wife had been feeling well during her recovery. She has never had an event like this one before.

Review of Systems:
* General: The patient had been feeling fine at home until today. She felt light-
headed in the shower before her episode.
*
Skin: She denies any rashes. She has bruising on her abdomen where she received injections
for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis during her recent hospitalization. Her right groin
incision site has not been painful, red, or purulent.
*
HEENT: Noncontributory
*
Pulmonary: Dyspnea at rest.
*
Cardiovascular: Constant, midsternal chest pain and pressure that does not radiate. No
palpitations before or after this morning's event.
*
Gastrointestinal: Noncontributory
*
Genitourinary: Noncontributory
*
Musculoskeletal: Denies pain in arms or legs.
*
Neurologic: Feels light-headed with standing. No vision changes, focal weakness, or other
neurologic symptoms.

*
Psychiatric: History of mild dementia with intermittent forgetfulness. Her husband states that her
dementia did not seem worse before today's event but she now seems confused.

Past Medical History:
* Medical history: Hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and aortic stenosis (severe).
*
Surgical history: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement 1-wk prior.
*
Medications: Clopidogrel, aspirin, docusate, multivitamins, and estrogen cream.
*
Allergies: No known drug allergies.
*
Family history: Noncontributory
*
Social history: Limited exercise tolerance. No recent travel. No history of drug or alcohol abuse.

Physical Examination:
* General appearance: Ill-appearing, confused elderly woman in respiratory
distress.
*
Vital signs:
* Temperature: 34.6° C
* Pulse: 115 beats/min, regular
* BP: 70/21 mmHg
* Respirations: 34/min
*
Skin: Face plethoric, cyanotic, and mottled. Extremities mottled. Multiple small ecchymoses on
lower abdomen compatible with history of recent anticoagulant injections. Groin incision healing
well, no bleeding.
*
HEENT: Significant bilateral jugular venous distention to angle of jaw.
*
Pulmonary: Shallow, rapid respirations; lung sounds clear and equal bilaterally; normal to
percussion bilaterally.
*

Cardiovascular: Tachycardia, mid-systolic mechanical click consistent with mechanical aortic
valve. Heart sounds muffled. Femoral and carotid pulses weak but symmetric. Unable to palpate
more distal pulses. Chest nontender, no crepitance with palpation.
*
Gastrointestinal: Unremarkable, including rectal exam showing stool brown and guaiac-
negative.
*
Genitourinary: Unremarkable
*
Musculoskeletal: No swelling, erythema, tenderness, or deformities of extremities.
*
Neurologic: Patient is unable to cooperate with detailed examination, but pupils are symmetric
and react equally to light, face appears symmetric, gag reflex is normal, and all extremities
move equally on command.
*
Mental status: Oriented only to name. Appears confused.

Test Results:
Results of appropriate testing return and show the following:
Bedside glucose level: 72 mg/dL
Pulse oximetry: 85% on room air; increases to 92% after giving oxygen
BP improves to 80/35 mm Hg with administration of 1 L fluid bolus.

Results of appropriate testing return and show the following:
Chest x-ray: Slight enlargement of the cardiac silhouette, otherwise unremarkable
ECG: Sinus tachycardia, normal voltage, no ST-T wave abnormalities, no electrical alternans

interpretation of this echocardiogram? (Please select one choice.)

Dilated right ventricle

Normal

Pericardial effusion

Pericardial thickening

Vignette: A 45-year-old man who plays recreational basketball on weekends presents with a 10-day history of right knee pain and intermittent mechanical symptoms. He reports that during a game he twisted his knee while landing from a jump and felt a sharp pain on the medial side. Since then, he has experienced episodes of the knee locking in a slightly flexed position and a catching sensation during walking. There is mild intermittent swelling. He denies instability or giving way. On examination, there is a small effusion and tenderness along the medial joint line. McMurray test produces a palpable click with pain on the medial side during external rotation. Thessaly test at 20 degrees is positive. The knee is stable to varus and valgus stress. Lachman test is negative.

Vignette:
A 45-year-old man who plays recreational basketball on weekends presents with a 10-day history of right knee pain and intermittent mechanical symptoms. He reports that during a game he twisted his knee while landing from a jump and felt a sharp pain on the medial side. Since then, he has experienced episodes of the knee locking in a slightly flexed position and a catching sensation during walking. There is mild intermittent swelling. He denies instability or giving way. On examination, there is a small effusion and tenderness along the medial joint line. McMurray test produces a palpable click with pain on the medial side during external rotation. Thessaly test at 20 degrees is positive. The knee is stable to varus and valgus stress. Lachman test is negative.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 45-year-old
Sex: Man
Complaint: 10-day history of right knee pain with intermittent mechanical locking and catching after a twisting injury sustained during recreational basketball.
Analysis: The presentation is highly consistent with a medial meniscal tear. The strongest supporting facts are the twisting mechanism, mechanical symptoms (locking and catching), medial joint line tenderness, small effusion, and positive meniscal provocation tests—specifically a McMurray test producing a palpable medial click with external rotation and a positive Thessaly test at 20 degrees. The negative Lachman test and absence of instability or giving way make an ACL rupture unlikely. Stability to varus and valgus stress effectively rules out significant collateral ligament injury. The main relevant differential considerations include an osteochondral fracture or an intra-articular loose body, though the localized medial examination findings strongly favor meniscal pathology.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: MRI of the right knee; plain radiographs (X-ray) of the right knee.
Conclusion: Medial meniscal tear with mechanical symptoms, likely involving an unstable or displaced fragment, with clinically intact ACL and collateral ligaments.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Obtain an MRI of the right knee to confirm the medial meniscal tear, characterize its pattern and location, assess for displacement, and evaluate for associated chondral or osteochondral injury. Refer to orthopedic surgery or sports medicine for definitive management; arthroscopic intervention should be anticipated given the mechanical locking episodes. In the interim, advise strict activity modification with avoidance of pivoting, jumping, and deep knee flexion; use of intermittent ice and NSAIDs if tolerated; and a hinged knee brace if locking recurs. Explicitly counsel the patient that an acutely locked knee that cannot be passively extended requires urgent reassessment.

Vignette:
A 12-year-old female presents with dry, itchy skin that involves the flexures in front of her elbows, behind her knees, and in front of her ankles. Her cheeks also have patches of dry, scaly skin. She has symptoms of hay fever and has recently been diagnosed with egg and milk allergy. She has a brother with asthma and an uncle and several cousins who have been diagnosed with eczema.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 12-year-old
Sex: Female
Complaint: Dry, itchy skin involving the flexures in front of the elbows, behind the knees, and in front of the ankles, with dry, scaly patches on the cheeks; accompanied by hay fever, egg allergy, and milk allergy.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for atopic dermatitis. The strongest supporting facts are the chronic pruritic, dry, scaly plaques in characteristic childhood flexural distribution (antecubital and popliteal fossae, ankles) and on the cheeks, combined with a robust personal and family atopic history: the patient has allergic rhinitis and IgE-mediated food allergies (egg and milk), her brother has asthma, and multiple relatives have eczema. The main differential considerations include allergic or irritant contact dermatitis and psoriasis. Psoriasis typically favors extensor surfaces with well-demarcated, silvery-scaled plaques, which differs from this flexural and facial pattern. Scabies is unlikely because there are no burrows or nodular lesions and the symmetric, chronic distribution does not fit an acute infestation. Papular urticaria, insect bites, and folliculitis are inconsistent with the morphology and distribution, as there are no wheals, central puncta, or follicular pustules described.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) in a patient with a strong personal and family history of atopy.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Initiate daily skin care with liberal application of fragrance-free emollients and gentle, non-soap cleansers; use lukewarm water for bathing. Treat acute flares with appropriate-potency topical corticosteroids (lower potency for facial lesions, medium potency for body flexures) for limited durations, with topical calcineurin inhibitors as steroid-sparing options for sensitive areas. Consider wet-wrap therapy for more significant flares. Manage pruritus with antihistamines if sleep is disturbed. Avoid known skin irritants such as harsh soaps, wool, and overheating. Coordinate ongoing care with her allergist regarding hay fever and confirmed egg and milk allergies; do not initiate unsupervised elimination diets, as dietary allergens may not be driving the skin disease. Educate the family on the chronic relapsing nature of the condition, proper application of topical therapies, and warning signs of secondary bacterial infection (increasing erythema, oozing, honey-colored crusting, or pustules).
Notes: Food allergies can coexist with atopic dermatitis but are not always direct triggers of skin flares; dietary management should remain under allergist supervision to prevent unnecessary restriction.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 20 years old
Sex: Male
Complaint: Persistent fatigue, sore throat, low-grade fevers, left upper quadrant abdominal discomfort, and swollen neck glands for 2 weeks; concern about returning to varsity lacrosse contact sports.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for infectious mononucleosis (IM) caused by Epstein-Barr virus. The strongest supporting facts are the positive heterophile antibody test (monospot), CBC showing lymphocytosis with 15% atypical lymphocytes, palpable splenomegaly 3 cm below the costal margin, bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and pharyngeal erythema with tonsillar exudates. The presence of splenomegaly in a contact-sport athlete raises immediate concern for splenic rupture risk and necessitates strict activity modification.

A 55-year-old man presents with a gradual decrease in hearing in his left ear over the past 2 weeks. He describes a sensation of fullness and occasional mild tinnitus in the affected ear. He admits to regular use of cotton swabs for ear cleaning. He denies ear pain, discharge, dizziness, or hearing loss in the right ear. He has no history of ear surgery or chronic ear infections. baseline_protocol:
Age: 55
Sex: Male
Complaint: Gradual left-sided hearing loss over 2 weeks with aural fullness and occasional mild tinnitus.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for conductive hearing loss secondary to cerumen impaction. Otoscopy reveals the left ear canal is completely occluded by dark brown cerumen, preventing visualization of the tympanic membrane and directly accounting for the hearing loss, fullness, and tinnitus. Regular cotton swab use is a known risk factor for distal cerumen compaction. The normal right ear and the absence of otalgia, otorrhea, vertigo, or history of chronic ear disease make infectious, inflammatory, and inner ear etiologies unlikely. While middle ear pathology cannot be definitively ruled out until the canal is cleared, the findings are overwhelmingly consistent with an external canal obstructive process. Less likely differentials include a foreign body or canal cholesteatoma, though the characteristic appearance and history favor impacted earwax.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Audiometry (to be performed after cerumen removal to document hearing thresholds and confirm resolution of the conductive deficit).
Conclusion: Left external auditory canal cerumen impaction causing conductive hearing loss, aural fullness, and mild tinnitus.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: 1) Remove the impacted cerumen using an appropriate method such as cerumenolytic drops, microsuction, or manual curettage under direct visualization; avoid blind instrumentation given the inability to assess tympanic membrane integrity. 2) Perform post-removal otoscopy to inspect the tympanic membrane and exclude underlying middle ear or canal pathology. 3) Obtain audiometry after canal clearance to confirm recovery of hearing. 4) Counsel the patient to immediately discontinue cotton swab use and refrain from inserting any objects into the ear canal; reinforce that ear canals are self-cleaning. 5) If hearing loss, fullness, or tinnitus persists

Vignette:
A 55-year-old male professional painter presents with a 4-month history of progressively worsening right shoulder pain. The pain is dull and aching, localized to the lateral deltoid region, and significantly worse when reaching overhead or behind his back. He reports difficulty sleeping on his right side. He has been painting houses for over 25 years with extensive overhead work. He denies any acute injury, numbness, or weakness. On examination, there is tenderness over the greater tuberosity. Active range of motion shows a painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees of abduction. The Neer impingement sign and Hawkins-Kennedy test are positive. Empty can test elicits pain but strength is preserved at 5 out of 5. External rotation strength is intact.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 55
Sex: Male
Complaint: 4-month history of progressively worsening dull, aching right shoulder pain localized to the lateral deltoid region, markedly aggravated by overhead reaching and reaching behind the back, with difficulty sleeping on the right side, in a professional painter with 25 years of overhead work.
Analysis: The findings are most consistent with subacromial impingement syndrome with underlying supraspinatus tendinopathy. The strongest supporting facts are the chronic progressive course in an overhead manual laborer; the painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees of abduction; tenderness over the greater tuberosity; positive Neer and Hawkins-Kennedy impingement signs; and a painful Empty can test with preserved 5/5 strength, indicating tendon irritability without functional discontinuity. Intact external rotation strength argues against significant infraspinatus or posterior cuff pathology. The absence of acute trauma, numbness, or weakness makes an acute traumatic rotator cuff tear or cervical radiculopathy unlikely. Adhesive capsulitis is unlikely given preserved active motion and intact external rotation. Glenohumeral osteoarthritis and acromioclavicular joint pathology are less consistent with the localized lateral deltoid symptoms and classic impingement signs.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Plain radiographs of the right shoulder (AP and outlet/Y-scapular views) to assess acromial morphology, the acromiohumeral interval, and calcific deposits. If symptoms persist or fail to improve with conservative care, consider musculoskeletal ultrasound or MRI to exclude a partial-thickness rotator cuff tear.
Conclusion: Chronic subacromial impingement syndrome with supraspinatus tendinopathy in a 55-year-old painter; no clinical evidence of a full-thickness rotator cuff tear.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: 1) Work modification: reduce sustained overhead painting and reaching behind the back; use ergonomic positioning to keep tasks below 90 degrees of shoulder abduction when feasible. 2) Sleep hygiene: avoid lying on the right side. 3) Initiate supervised physical therapy focused on rotator cuff strengthening (particularly supraspinatus and infraspinatus), scapular stabilization, and posterior capsule stretching. 4) Analgesia with acetaminophen or NSAIDs if no contraindications. 5) Consider a subacromial corticosteroid injection if pain limits participation in rehabilitation. 6) Obtain the recommended plain radiographs as the initial imaging study. 7) Re-evaluate in 6 to 12 weeks; if there is no meaningful improvement or if weakness develops, obtain MRI to assess for partial- or full-thickness rotator cuff tear before considering operative intervention.
Notes: None

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery

Initiate broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation for suspected mediastinitis and pleural sepsis given documented fever, hypotension, tachycardia, and hypoxemia. Place a left-sided chest tube to drain the contaminated pleural effusion. Provide supplemental oxygen, analgesia, and close hemodynamic and respiratory monitoring. Additional considerations include the high risk of rapid clinical deterioration from mediastinal sepsis and the need to avoid any further oral intake or imaging contrast agents given the confirmed extravasation.

Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
